messages.subject: issue with shiny progress indicator
parts:
Dear group:
I am trying to use either withProgress or progressObject to show a long calculation by a external function (Traitsmodel).

This is the code for using withProgress:
withProgress(
      TraitModel(jobtime, 1, fileName_param, fileName_substrates, fileName_inputs, outFile),
      min=1, max =20, message = 'Calculation in progress',
      detail = 'This may take a while...',
      for (i in 1:15) {
        incProgress(1/15)
        Sys.sleep(0.1)
      }
    )

I have the message showed up but I don't see a moving bar.

Now with ProgressObject:
progress <- shiny::Progress$new(session, min=1, max=15)
    on.exit(progress$close())
    
    progress$set(message = 'Calculation in progress',
                detail = 'This may take a while...')
    
    for (i in 1:20) {
      progress$set(value = i)
      Sys.sleep(0.1)
    }
    TraitModel(jobtime, 1, fileName_param, fileName_substrates, fileName_inputs, outFile)

The bar moved to the end before the calculation finished. 

Assume we do not break down the TraitsModel function down to smaller pieces what will be my best option to show progress?

Thanks!

Ping

messages.author: 2674b6f8d9871f58
messages.subject: Re: issue with shiny progress indicator
parts:
Your first code makes no sense. The TraitsModel call is the "expr" argument to withProgress, the function that will be evaluated and is expected to contain calls to incProgress or setProgress. It presumably doesn't, so that's why your bar isn't working very well. The for (i in 1:20) code seems to be being passed to withProgress as the session argument, which might cause weird behaviour.

In your second example, it should be no surprise that the bar completes before your function is called, because that's exactly what you've told it to do. You set the message and detail, then your for loop runs and increments the bar to max, then TraitsModel is called. You need to do this some other way.

The fundamental problem with this approach is that you're relying on Sys.sleep though. This approach makes no sense because you have no idea how long TraitsModel will take. Maybe your machine will get a hardware upgrade and the code will suddenly be much faster, or maybe there will be heavy load when the user happens to run the function and it takes much longer than expected. A simple time-based progress bar doesn't make much sense in this context. If there aren't obvious points inside TraitsModel where you could increment the bar, it might be better to just use a spinner so that the user understands that something is happening, but that they still have to wait.
